chunks: And from him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il ibn Bazee', who said:

I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about a woman who made her slave-girl permissible for me, and he said: 'That is for you.' I said: 'But what if she is joking?' He said: 'How is it with you regarding what is in her heart? If you know that she is joking, then it is not (permissible).'

As for what Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Yaqteen from his brother al-Husayn ibn Ali ibn Yaqteen, who said: I asked him about a man who makes the private part of his slave-girl permissible for him, he said: 'I do not like that.'

So in it is not that which necessitates the prohibition of what we mentioned, because it came in the place of dislike (karahah), and the Imam (peace be upon him) explicitly stated that with his saying 'I do not like that'. The reason for the dislike of that is that this is something which others besides us do not consider, and among those who criticize us for it are our opponents, so abstaining from what this path is is more preferable.
And it is permissible that he only disliked that if it was not stipulated in the child that he be free (hur), so as for if it was stipulated, then the dislike has also departed from it.
And that which indicates this is what was narrated:

key_terms.الْكَرَاهَةِ: dislike (a juristic status between permissible and forbidden)
key_terms.يُحِلُّ فَرْجَ: makes permissible the private part (of a slave-girl)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a man having relations with a slave-girl if the woman who granted her was joking?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* elucidates the juristic nuances of *Tamlik al-Qinayah* (granting a slave-girl for sexual use), distinguishing between the validity of the grant based on the grantor's intent (serious vs. joking) and the broader scholarly preference (*karahah*) for this practice. Al-Tusi contextualizes the dislike as a matter of *ihtiyat* (prudence) to avoid criticism from opposing schools (*mu'takhalifuna*) regarding the status of offspring, while noting that stipulating the child's freedom removes this objection, aligning with the Shia principle of ensuring legitimate lineage.
